overview: ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) is a data integration pattern where raw data is extracted from sources and loaded immediately into a powerful target warehouse or data lake, then transformed IN-PLACE using the target system's own compute.

The defining characteristic of ELT is that transformation happens AFTER the load, so raw data is retained in the target and transformations are expressed as SQL/transformation models that run on the warehouse engine.

ELT is the dominant modern cloud pattern, enabled by elastic, cheap, scalable engines like Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift, and Databricks, typically orchestrated with dbt for the Transform layer.
learningObjectives: Understand the three phases of ELT and why transformation follows loading in modern cloud architectures.
Identify the cloud warehouses/lakehouses and tools (dbt, Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks) that make ELT practical.
Contrast ELT with ETL and articulate the pros, cons, and decision criteria an interviewer expects.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: ELT is a three-stage data pipeline process in which data is extracted from source systems and loaded in its raw form into a target data warehouse or data lake, after which transformations (cleansing, joins, aggregations, business logic) are applied in-place using the target system's compute engine. Transformation occurs after the load, and raw data is persisted in the target.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: ELT is like buying all your groceries and putting them straight into a giant, powerful smart kitchen (the warehouse). You only chop, cook, and season them when you actually need a particular dish, using the kitchen's own appliances. Because all the raw ingredients are still in the kitchen, you can cook many different dishes from them later.
coreConcept.historicalContext: ELT became viable in the 2010s with the rise of cloud data warehouses that separate storage from elastic compute and offer massive parallel processing at low cost (Redshift in 2012, BigQuery, Snowflake from 2014). Suddenly the warehouse itself was powerful and cheap enough to do the transformations, removing the need for a separate ETL engine. Tools like dbt (2016) popularized SQL-based, version-controlled, in-warehouse transformations, cementing ELT as the modern default.

whyItMatters.business: ELT shortens time-to-data: raw data lands quickly and analysts can derive new metrics on demand without re-engineering pipelines, accelerating analytics and experimentation.
whyItMatters.engineering: Engineers maintain a simpler architecture (no separate transform tier), express transformations as version-controlled SQL, and let the warehouse handle scaling automatically.
whyItMatters.scalability: Elastic cloud warehouses scale compute up and down on demand, so large transformations run on the same engine that serves queries, with massively parallel processing.
whyItMatters.cost: Pay-per-use cloud compute and cheap object storage make it economical to store all raw data and transform only what's needed, when it's needed.
whyItMatters.reliability: Because raw data is retained, transformations are reproducible and re-runnable; a logic bug can be fixed and the models simply re-run against the preserved raw data.

coreComponents.name: Extract
coreComponents.definition: The stage that reads raw data from source systems such as databases, APIs, event streams, files, and SaaS apps.
coreComponents.purpose: To capture source data, often via managed connectors, with minimal processing.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Connect to sources, support full and incremental extraction, and deliver raw data to the loader without heavy transformation.
coreComponents.examples: Fivetran/Airbyte connectors pulling from Salesforce, Stripe, or a Postgres database.

coreComponents.name: Load
coreComponents.definition: The stage that writes raw, minimally processed data directly into the target warehouse or lake (often a raw/landing schema).
coreComponents.purpose: To get source data into the powerful target system quickly and preserve it in raw form.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Bulk-load into raw tables, manage schema evolution, handle incremental appends/merges, and retain raw history.
coreComponents.examples: COPY into a Snowflake `raw` schema, streaming inserts into a BigQuery dataset, writing Parquet to a Delta Lake bronze table.

coreComponents.name: Transform
coreComponents.definition: The stage that applies cleansing, joins, business logic, and aggregation IN-PLACE using the target's compute, after the data is loaded.
coreComponents.purpose: To turn raw loaded data into clean, modeled, analysis-ready tables (staging, marts) on demand.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Express transformations as SQL/transformation models (e.g., dbt), manage dependencies/lineage, materialize views/tables, and test outputs.
coreComponents.examples: dbt models building staging -> intermediate -> mart layers inside Snowflake/BigQuery.

internalWorking: Managed connectors (Fivetran, Airbyte, Stitch) or custom extractors pull raw data and load it into a raw/landing schema in the cloud warehouse, preserving source fidelity.
Transformation tools like dbt compile a DAG of SQL models, resolving dependencies between staging, intermediate, and mart layers.
Each model is executed as SQL on the warehouse's massively parallel compute, materialized as a view, table, or incremental table inside the target.
Tests and freshness checks validate the transformed outputs; orchestration (dbt Cloud, Airflow, Dagster) schedules runs and the warehouse auto-scales compute for the workload.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Source Systems -> Extract -> Load (raw schema in warehouse/lake) -> Transform in-place (SQL/dbt on warehouse compute) -> Modeled tables/marts
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A Fivetran connector extracts new Stripe charges and loads them as-is into the `raw.stripe_charges` table in Snowflake.
2. A dbt staging model `stg_charges` casts types, renames columns, and standardizes the raw data into a clean view.
3. A dbt mart model joins `stg_charges` to customers and aggregates to `fct_daily_revenue`, running as SQL on Snowflake's elastic warehouse.
4. dbt tests assert uniqueness and non-null keys; if they pass, downstream BI tools query the modeled tables. Raw data remains in `raw` for any future re-derivation.

keyTerminology.meaning: Raw data is loaded first and interpreted/structured only when transformed or queried, with a preserved raw layer.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables fast loading and lets you re-derive new models later from retained raw data.

keyTerminology.meaning: A SQL-based transformation framework that builds, tests, documents, and version-controls in-warehouse models as a DAG.
keyTerminology.importance: The de facto standard for the Transform layer in modern ELT stacks.

keyTerminology.meaning: A layered modeling approach (bronze/raw, silver/cleaned, gold/aggregated) common in lakehouse ELT.
keyTerminology.importance: Provides a clear pattern for progressively transforming raw data in-place.

importantConcepts.explanation: The hallmark of ELT: raw data is loaded first, then transformed in-place, keeping raw data available and pushing compute onto the elastic warehouse.
Modern cloud warehouses decouple cheap storage from elastic compute, which is what makes loading all raw data and transforming on demand economical and scalable.

variationsAndTypes: **SQL/dbt ELT:** Transformations expressed as version-controlled SQL models run inside Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift.
**Lakehouse ELT (medallion):** Raw data lands in a lake (Delta/Iceberg), transformed progressively bronze -> silver -> gold on Spark/Databricks.
**Incremental ELT:** Models materialize incrementally, transforming only new/changed rows for cost and speed.
advantages: **Fast ingestion:** Raw data lands immediately with little upfront engineering, so data is available sooner.
**Flexibility / re-derivation:** Retained raw data lets analysts build new transformations later without re-extracting.
**Simpler architecture:** No separate transformation tier; the warehouse does both transform and serve.
**Scales with the warehouse:** Elastic cloud compute and SQL/dbt make transformations easy to scale and maintain.
disadvantages: **Raw/sensitive data in the target:** PII lands in the warehouse, requiring masking, governance, and access controls there.
**Warehouse compute cost:** Heavy in-warehouse transformations consume billable compute and can be expensive if uncontrolled.
**Requires a powerful target:** ELT depends on an elastic, high-performance warehouse; weak/legacy targets cannot handle it well.
**Governance burden:** Storing all raw data increases the surface area for data governance, lineage, and compliance management.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use ELT when you have a powerful elastic cloud warehouse/lakehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift), want fast time-to-data, value retaining raw data for future re-derivation, and want analysts/analytics engineers to iterate on transformations rapidly with SQL/dbt.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid ELT when the target lacks elastic compute, when strict compliance requires that PII never lands in the warehouse, when warehouse compute is the dominant cost and transformations are heavy/constant, or when working with legacy on-premise warehouses better served by ETL.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: ELT is like a warehouse store that stocks every raw product and only assembles or customizes orders on demand right there in the store using its own machines. Because all the raw stock is already on-site, the store can fulfill many different custom orders later without re-ordering supplies.

commonMisconceptions.myth: ELT means no transformation, just dumping data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: ELT still transforms data thoroughly — it just does so after loading, in-place on the warehouse, typically as well-tested SQL/dbt models. The data is just as modeled as in ETL.

commonMisconceptions.myth: ELT is always cheaper than ETL.
commonMisconceptions.reality: ELT shifts compute onto billable warehouse resources. For heavy, constant transformations it can be more expensive than transforming on a cheaper external engine; cost depends on workload and pricing model.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Leverage the warehouse's elastic compute and separation of storage/compute to scale transformations. Use incremental models, partitioning/clustering, and right-sized virtual warehouses to handle growth.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Because raw data is retained, transformations are reproducible: fix a model and re-run it against preserved raw data. Use idempotent incremental logic and dbt tests as quality gates.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Loads and transforms can be retried safely when made idempotent. The raw layer acts as a durable checkpoint so transform failures never require re-extraction.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Monitor warehouse credit/compute consumption, model run times, dbt test results, source freshness, and DAG run success to catch cost spikes and data-quality regressions.
productionConsiderations.security: Because raw PII lands in the warehouse, enforce column-level masking, row-level security, role-based access, and encryption; restrict access to the raw layer.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Use incremental materializations, auto-suspend/auto-scale virtual warehouses, partition pruning, and materialize only frequently queried models to control compute spend.
productionConsiderations.performance: Tune clustering/partitioning keys, prefer set-based SQL, use incremental models to avoid full rebuilds, and size virtual warehouses appropriately for each workload.

codeExamples.title: A dbt Staging Model (Transform-in-place SQL)
codeExamples.overview: This dbt model transforms raw loaded Stripe charges into a clean, typed staging view inside the warehouse — the Transform stage of ELT.
codeExamples.code:
-- models/staging/stg_charges.sql
-- Raw data was already LOADED into raw.stripe_charges by Fivetran.

with source as (
    select * from {{ source('stripe', 'charges') }}
),

cleaned as (
    select
        id                          as charge_id,
        customer                    as customer_id,
        amount / 100.0              as amount_usd,
        upper(currency)             as currency,
        case when status = 'succeeded' then true else false end as is_paid,
        to_timestamp(created)       as created_at
    from source
    where created is not null
)

select * from cleaned
codeExamples.breakdown: The `source()` function references the already-loaded raw Stripe table — extraction and loading happened upstream via a connector. The model then cleans and types the data (renames columns, converts cents to dollars, normalizes currency, derives an is_paid flag) entirely as SQL executed on the warehouse. This is transformation-after-load, the essence of ELT.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A `stg_charges` view (or table) in the warehouse with clean, typed columns: charge_id, customer_id, amount_usd, currency, is_paid, created_at.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting to declare the `source` in `sources.yml` causes compilation errors. Doing heavy joins in a view materialization can be slow; consider materializing as a table. Dividing integer cents without casting to float can truncate amounts.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Materialize high-traffic models as tables or incremental models, cluster/partition on date keys, and keep staging models thin (rename/cast only), pushing joins to downstream marts.

codeExamples.title: An Incremental dbt Mart Model
codeExamples.overview: This incremental dbt model aggregates clean charges into a daily-revenue fact, transforming only new data each run to save warehouse compute.
codeExamples.breakdown: The `incremental` materialization means dbt only processes rows newer than what's already in the table on subsequent runs (the `is_incremental()` block filters by date). It references the upstream `stg_charges` model via `ref()`, building a dependency DAG. The aggregation runs on the warehouse's parallel compute — transformation in-place.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A `fct_daily_revenue` table with one row per (revenue_date, currency) containing total_revenue and charge_count, updated incrementally each run.
codeExamples.commonIssues: If `unique_key` is wrong, incremental runs can duplicate rows. Late-arriving data before the max date can be missed without a lookback window. Schema changes in raw require handling on_schema_change.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Add a small lookback window to capture late data, set on_schema_change appropriately, and partition/cluster the table by revenue_date for efficient incremental merges.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A SaaS startup wants a same-day analytics platform showing daily revenue and active customers, built quickly by a small data team using a cloud warehouse, without standing up a separate ETL cluster.
endToEndExample.inputData: Raw event and billing data from Stripe (charges, subscriptions) and the product Postgres database (users, accounts), extracted via Fivetran.
endToEndExample.architecture: Fivetran extracts and loads raw data into a `raw` schema in Snowflake; dbt transforms it in-place into staging and mart layers; BI tools (Looker) query the marts. dbt Cloud orchestrates scheduled runs.
processingSteps: 1. Extract & Load: Fivetran connectors pull Stripe and Postgres data and load raw tables into Snowflake's `raw` schema on a schedule.
2. Stage: dbt staging models clean and type the raw tables (rename, cast, normalize).
3. Model: dbt mart models join and aggregate staged data into `fct_daily_revenue` and `dim_customers` using Snowflake compute.
4. Test: dbt tests assert uniqueness, non-null keys, and accepted values; source freshness is checked.
5. Serve: BI tools query the gold/mart tables; raw data is retained for future re-modeling.
endToEndExample.output: Modeled `fct_daily_revenue` and `dim_customers` tables in Snowflake, refreshed on schedule, with raw source data preserved in the `raw` schema for any future metric.
endToEndExample.monitoring: dbt Cloud reports model run status and test failures; Snowflake monitors warehouse credit usage; source freshness alerts fire if a connector falls behind.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Failed loads are retried by the connector; failed dbt tests block downstream models and alert the team; because raw data is retained, a buggy model is fixed and simply re-run with no re-extraction.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The small team ships same-day analytics with minimal infrastructure; new metrics can be added by writing new dbt models against retained raw data, demonstrating ELT's speed and flexibility.

industryUseCases.company: Modern SaaS Companies (e.g., Notion, Canva-style startups)
industryUseCases.problem: Building analytics fast with a small data team and no appetite to operate a separate ETL cluster.
industryUseCases.solution: Fivetran/Airbyte load raw SaaS and app data into Snowflake/BigQuery; dbt transforms in-place into modeled marts.
industryUseCases.benefits: Rapid time-to-data, simple architecture, analyst-friendly SQL transformations, and retained raw data for new metrics.

industryUseCases.problem: Combining clickstream, orders, and marketing data for flexible, evolving analytics.
industryUseCases.solution: Load raw events and orders into BigQuery, then build dbt models progressively (staging -> marts) leveraging BigQuery's elastic compute.
industryUseCases.benefits: Analysts iterate on new funnels and cohorts on demand without re-engineering pipelines, using preserved raw event data.

industryUseCases.company: Data-Driven Enterprises using Lakehouse (e.g., Databricks customers)
industryUseCases.problem: Processing large, varied data (structured + semi-structured) for both BI and machine learning.
industryUseCases.solution: Land raw data in a Delta Lake bronze layer, transform progressively to silver/gold (medallion) using Spark SQL in-place.
industryUseCases.benefits: Unified storage for analytics and ML, scalable in-place transformation, and raw retention enabling reproducible pipelines.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Exploit separation of storage and compute: scale virtual warehouses/clusters elastically for transform workloads, use incremental models to bound work, and partition/cluster large tables. Multiple isolated warehouses prevent transform jobs from starving BI queries.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: The retained raw layer is a durable checkpoint — transform failures never require re-extraction. Idempotent incremental models and connector retries make loads and transforms safely re-runnable.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Cloud warehouses provide managed HA and durability; orchestrators (dbt Cloud, Airflow, Dagster) run in HA mode. Stateless dbt runs can be retried on any worker.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Cloud warehouse time-travel/cloning and object-storage durability protect raw data; because models are version-controlled SQL, the entire transformed layer can be rebuilt from retained raw data after an incident.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Use incremental materializations to avoid full rebuilds, cluster/partition on filter keys for pruning, prefer set-based SQL, materialize hot models as tables, and right-size warehouses per workload.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Auto-suspend idle warehouses, use incremental models, avoid unnecessary full refreshes, prune with partition/cluster keys, and monitor per-model credit consumption to catch expensive transformations.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Because raw PII lands in the warehouse, apply column-level masking policies, row-level security, role-based access control, and encryption, and tightly restrict access to the raw schema.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track warehouse credit usage, model run durations, dbt test pass rates, DAG run outcomes, and source freshness; alert on cost spikes, failed tests, and stale sources.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Use dbt tests (unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values) and freshness checks as gates so failing data blocks downstream models and is surfaced immediately.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Centralize dbt/orchestrator logs and run artifacts; alert on run failures, test failures, source-freshness breaches, and unexpected compute-cost increases.

recommendedPractices: **Preserve a raw layer:** Load raw data untransformed and keep it, enabling re-derivation of new models later.
**Layer your models:** Use staging -> intermediate -> mart (or bronze/silver/gold) for clarity and reuse.
**Use incremental models:** Transform only new/changed data to control compute cost and run time.
**Test transformations:** Add dbt tests as quality gates that block downstream models on failure.
engineeringStandards: All transformations must be version-controlled SQL/code with code review and CI.
PII landing in the warehouse must be protected with masking and access controls.
Incremental models must define a correct unique_key and handle late-arriving data.
designRecommendations: Keep staging models thin (rename/cast only); push joins and business logic to mart models.
Isolate transform compute from BI compute using separate virtual warehouses.
Document model lineage and expose it (dbt docs) for discoverability.
namingConventions: Use a `raw` schema for loaded source data and `analytics`/`marts` for modeled outputs.
documentationStandards: Document sources, freshness expectations, and each model's purpose in dbt YAML.
Maintain auto-generated lineage from raw sources through to marts.
Record which tests guard each model and the action on failure.
testingStrategies: Use schema tests (unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values) on key columns.
Add freshness checks on sources to detect stale loads.
Run dbt build in CI on pull requests to catch breaking model changes early.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting in-warehouse transformations run as full refreshes when they could be incremental.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Incremental logic is more complex, so teams default to rebuilding everything each run.
commonMistakes.impact: Runaway warehouse compute costs and long run times as data volume grows.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use incremental materializations with a correct unique_key and a small lookback window for late data.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring that raw PII now lives in the warehouse.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: ELT loads raw data first, and teams forget the governance implications of sensitive data landing in the target.
commonMistakes.impact: Compliance violations and unauthorized access to PII by analysts.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Apply column masking, row-level security, and role-based access, and restrict access to the raw schema.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting heavy business logic in views that are queried repeatedly.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Views are easy to create and feel cheap, but they re-execute logic on every query.
commonMistakes.impact: Slow dashboards and repeated, expensive warehouse compute.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Materialize frequently queried, expensive models as tables or incremental tables.

comparisonSection.optionA: ELT: Load raw first, Transform in-place after
comparisonSection.explanation: ELT loads raw data into the target and transforms it there afterward, retaining raw data. ETL transforms on a separate engine and loads only the finished result, so the target never holds raw data.

ELT uses the warehouse's elastic compute, simplifying architecture and letting analysts transform with SQL/dbt. ETL keeps heavy transformation off the warehouse, useful when warehouse compute is scarce or expensive.

comparisonSection.optionA: ELT: fast ingest, raw retained, more governance surface
comparisonSection.optionB: ETL: slower ingest, raw not retained, easier pre-load masking
comparisonSection.explanation: ELT lands data fast and keeps raw data for re-derivation, but PII in the warehouse increases governance burden. ETL is slower to ingest and harder to re-derive but makes it easy to mask/drop PII before it ever lands.

beginnerQuestions.question: What does ELT stand for and how does it differ from ETL?
beginnerQuestions.answer: ELT stands for Extract, Load, Transform. Raw data is extracted and loaded into the warehouse first, then transformed in-place using the warehouse's compute. ETL transforms data on a separate engine before loading. The difference is the order of Transform and Load and where the compute runs.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: State both the ordering difference (load then transform) and that ELT transforms in-place on the target.

beginnerQuestions.question: Why has ELT become the modern default for cloud data stacks?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Cloud warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) separate cheap storage from elastic compute and are powerful enough to transform data in-place. Combined with cheap storage to retain raw data and tools like dbt for SQL transformations, ELT offers faster time-to-data, flexibility, and a simpler architecture.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Tie ELT's rise to elastic cloud compute, cheap storage, and dbt.

intermediateQuestions.question: What are the main downsides of ELT?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Raw and sensitive data now lives in the warehouse, increasing governance and PII-protection burden; warehouse compute for transformations is billable and can be costly for heavy workloads; and ELT requires a powerful elastic target — weak or legacy warehouses can't handle it well.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Show balance: ELT is not universally better; cost and governance are real trade-offs.

intermediateQuestions.question: How does dbt fit into the ELT pattern?
intermediateQuestions.answer: dbt handles the Transform stage: it lets you write version-controlled SQL models that run in-place on the warehouse, manages a dependency DAG via ref(), supports incremental materializations, and provides testing, documentation, and lineage. It does not extract or load — connectors do that.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Clarify that dbt is transform-only and operates inside the warehouse.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you control warehouse compute costs in a large ELT pipeline?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use incremental models so only new data is transformed, auto-suspend/auto-scale virtual warehouses, partition/cluster tables for pruning, materialize only frequently queried models as tables, isolate transform compute from BI compute, and monitor per-model credit consumption to catch expensive models.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Cost control is the central operational concern of ELT — be specific.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you handle PII in an ELT architecture where raw data lands in the warehouse?
advancedQuestions.answer: Apply dynamic column-level masking policies and row-level security on raw tables, use role-based access control so only authorized roles see raw PII, encrypt data at rest and in transit, restrict the raw schema, and optionally tokenize or pseudonymize sensitive fields during transformation into the curated layer.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Acknowledge that ELT shifts PII into the warehouse and that governance there is mandatory.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A startup wants analytics live in a week with a two-person data team on Snowflake. Would you choose ETL or ELT, and how would you build it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Small team, tight timeline, and an elastic cloud warehouse favor minimal infrastructure and SQL-based work. ELT loads raw fast and lets the small team transform with dbt without operating a separate cluster.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Choose ELT: use Fivetran/Airbyte to load raw source data into a Snowflake `raw` schema, then build dbt staging and mart models that transform in-place, add dbt tests, and point BI at the marts. This delivers fast time-to-data with minimal infrastructure and retained raw data.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an ELT analytics platform for a company ingesting data from 10 SaaS apps and a transactional database into BigQuery.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Use managed connectors (Fivetran/Airbyte) to extract and load raw data into a BigQuery `raw` dataset. Build a layered dbt project (staging -> intermediate -> marts) that transforms in-place. Add dbt tests and source-freshness checks, orchestrate with dbt Cloud/Airflow, and serve marts to BI.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: ELT gives fast ingest, raw retention, and a simple architecture, but raw PII in BigQuery requires masking/access controls and transformation compute is billable. Heavy models should be incremental to control cost.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Use incremental models and partition/cluster on date keys for pruning; scale BigQuery slots or use separate reservations for transform vs. BI workloads; add new sources by adding connectors and dbt models without re-architecting.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: ELT extracts data, loads it raw into a powerful warehouse/lake, then transforms it in-place using the target's elastic compute — transform happens after load.
keyConcepts: Order: Extract -> Load -> Transform (transform after load, in-place).
Powered by elastic cloud warehouses: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks.
dbt is the standard Transform layer (version-controlled SQL models + tests).
Raw layer is retained, enabling re-derivation of new metrics.
Best when the target is powerful/elastic and fast time-to-data and flexibility matter.
formulas: N/A — ELT is a process pattern with no governing mathematical formula.
commands: fivetran/airbyte connector -> COPY into raw schema  # extract + load
interviewPoints: Transform AFTER load, in-place on the warehouse, is the defining trait of ELT.
Enabled by separation of storage and compute in cloud warehouses.
Pros: fast ingest, flexibility/raw retention, simple architecture.
Cons: PII in warehouse, billable compute, needs a powerful target.
dbt handles transform only; connectors do extract+load.
quickNotes: ELT is the modern cloud default but coexists with ETL.
Use incremental models to control warehouse compute cost.
Mask PII and apply RBAC because raw data lands in the warehouse.
Retained raw data makes pipelines reproducible and re-derivable.

keyTakeaways: ELT means Extract, Load, Transform — raw data is loaded into a powerful warehouse first and transformed in-place afterward.
It is the modern cloud default, enabled by elastic, cheap compute in Snowflake/BigQuery/Databricks and tools like dbt for SQL transformations.
The defining contrast with ETL is order and compute location: ELT loads raw then transforms inside the warehouse; ETL transforms externally before load.

ELT's strengths are fast time-to-data, flexibility, raw-data retention for re-derivation, and a simpler architecture; its costs are PII governance in the warehouse and billable transformation compute.
Control ELT cost with incremental models and warehouse tuning, and protect PII with masking and access controls since raw data now lives in the target.
